faqs.a: The annuity formula: FV = PV x (1+r)^n + PMT x ((1+r)^n - 1)/r, where r is the monthly rate and n the number of months. The first term grows your lump sum; the second grows your stream of monthly payments.
faqs.q: What is the future value formula?

faqs.a: Yes - set the lump sum to 0 and only monthly contributions count. Set monthly contributions to 0 and only the lump sum grows. Both can also work together.
faqs.q: Can I use only monthly payments, no lump sum?

faqs.a: Compounding is monthly: your annual rate is divided by 12. So 7% annual becomes about 0.5833% per month. A monthly-contribution model is more accurate for regular savers than annual compounding.

Mostly time. In the worked example below, 10 years at 7% turns $34,000 of contributions into $54,713. Stretch it to 20 years and the same contributions grow far more, because later years compound on an already-large balance.
faqs.q: Time vs amount - which matters more?

faqs.a: Use a conservative rate like 5-6% to see a safer range, then compare with 7-8% to see the upside. The gap between the two answers shows how sensitive your plan is to returns.
faqs.q: Which interest rate should I use?

faqs.a: No. This calculator is a planning tool, not a prediction. Real investments fluctuate, charge fees, and get taxed. Use it to compare plans, not to promise an outcome.

future-value-calculator.formula:
Monthly rate r = annual rate / 12, months n = years x 12
FV = lump sum x (1+r)^n + monthly payment x ((1+r)^n - 1) / r
Contributions = lump sum + monthly payment x n
Growth (interest) = FV - contributions
howTo: Enter your starting lump sum (0 if you are starting from scratch).
Enter how much you will add each month.
Enter the expected annual return and the number of years.
Read the future value, your total contributions, and the growth separately.
Adjust years or the monthly amount to compare plans.
keyFacts: Future value = what your money grows into at a given rate over time.
Two engines work at once: the lump sum compounds, and monthly payments compound too.
Monthly compounding matches how most people actually save.
Growth accelerates late: the last years add far more than the first.
Contributions vs growth are shown separately so you can see compounding at work.
